messages.subject: new ODE functions
parts:
[off issue]

We need to add the stiff ODE solver to the language, and so
need a name.

A. Current proposal is for four functions with two names (the
control params being optional):

integrate_ode_cvodes(...args..., ...control params...)
integrate_ode_cvodes_stiff(...args..., ...control params...);

B. An alternative, which I prefer, would be to drop "cvodes" from
the name and just go with

integrate_ode(...)
integrate_ode_stiff(...)

We'd then replace the Boost solver currently behind integrate_ode
with the CVODES non-stiff solver. Note that we don't name other
functions with the packages providing algorithms used to compute them!
But I seem to recall some issue with efficiency. Is the non-stiff
CVODES solver just overall better rthan the Runge-Kutta implementation
in Boost?

C. Add in the algorithm name, rather than implementation pacakge:

integrate_ode_adams_moulton(...)

and so on. I don't even know what these are, but they might be more
familiar to users than "cvodes".


Any preferences?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: new ODE functions
parts:
Hi!

I agree that the specific implementation (CVODES) is not so of interest to the user. I am suggesting a blend of the above:

- we have two simple go-to default functions for users:

integrate_ode => non-stiff
integrate_ode_stiff => stiff

These functions set the default abs+rel tol and maximum number of steps.

- Additionally, we have functions with more control which are named for their algorithm:

integrate_ode_rk45
integrate_ode_adams_moulton
integrate_ode_bdf

These functions would take extra arguments for abs+rel tol and maximum number of steps.

This way we would have covered expert users and normal mortals. This would also be in line with what I see in other ODE packages, i.e. they make the options named after the algorithm.

I would prefer to keep the rk45 from boost in addition to the adams_moulton from CVODES. The material is far to complex for me to exhaustively cover this with benchmark tests to decide which one is really better and I do think this will actually always depend on the exact model, etc.. RK45 is around for ages as is adams_moulton. Moreover, adams_moulton is advertised as requiring fewer calls to the ODE RHS and the sensitivity ODE RHS. From that angle adams_moulton should be better than RK45, since it avoids a few calls to AD.

If you think getting rid of boost odeint is a big advantage, then so be it.

Best,
Sebastian

parts: I like your proposal

> integrate_ode => non-stiff

> integrate_ode_rk45
> integrate_ode_adams_moulton

There are sizeable advantages to having fewer functions for both
users and developers.

For users, there's much less to read and many fewer decisions to
make, so much less chance of being overwhelmed by detail or being
tempted into trying all the options. Of course, this only makes sense if expert
users don't need to make those decisions.

On the dev side, fewer functions and code dependencies means
proportionally less doc, testing, and ongoing maintenance.

- Bob

Hmm... your arguments make sense. Also, thinking about how much code could go away if we remove the odeint RK45 integrator...that's quite a lot of code+testing code. From that perspective going with CVODES only is a big win, true. Ok, even though this won't cover everything I will fire off tomorrow a benchmark for a non-stiff problem which takes 2-3 days. I only think that this naming scheme is not really expandable (and only experts use it, so it's fine to have the names), but maybe that is just a minor point. As I have been exposed to these things so much, I like my details; but maybe they don't matter so much in the end. Bottom line: I can live with your option A.

Sebastian

Sebastian

Hi Daniel!

To clarify what point 2: Yesterday we merge a replacement of the CVODE library with CVODES library, not more. So for stiff problems the integrate_ode_cvode function is still using the old approach of exposing the coupled_ode system to the cvode ode solver, but ignoring the extra capeabilities of CVODES. What needs to be merge is the pull request 283 on math for which I still owe you some documentation and a final review.

So currently the stiff solver in Stan is not fun to work with. In fact the non-stiff system I used for benchmarks of odeint freezes the integrate_ode_cvode function as it is right now. Only when you switch to the intgrate_ode_cvodes function it works.

So for stiff there is still a huge gain by switching to integrate_ode_cvodes.

Sebastian

Clean is a relative concept. We really don't want unused
files, large blocks of commented out code, etc. Also, code
that's checked in should run for others and not depend on features
of a local environment. All that requires some degree of cleaning.

I always start with a repo or branch and try to keep everything
"clean" as I go. I find it's easier in the long run that way,
sort of like cleaning as you go when cooking a large meal.

We're less picky for test/benchmark code than for the Stan code
itself.

Hi!

My benchmarks tests are somewhat specialized to our computing environment. So I use a system like

1. An R script which sets up simulated data, inits and everything else what is needed to kick off a Stan run. This is the "model" file as I call it.

2. Another R script which takes the model file, parses it, creates a sub-directory, serializes the data into that directory, copies the stan source and executable into it, sets up init files and finally creates "fit.sh" and optionally "post.sh".

3. then I submit things into the SGE cluster queue

However, the script fit.sh can be called from the command line like

./fit.sh

(trivial). This will start chain id 1; if you want chain X then you do

SGE_TASK_ID=X ./fit.sh

Is that too "local" or would that suffices to linger in one of the stan repos?

Sebastian

Putting things into the stan github raises the bar a bit for me - I don't always go forward with clean code (although I put quite some tests in my code) and before I share code some polishing should be done...
